strengths: Introduces S2R-HDR, the first large-scale synthetic HDR fusion dataset (24,000 samples), representing roughly a 6x scale increase over the largest prior paired ground-truth dataset (Challenge123, 123 samples) and addressing a genuine bottleneck in the HDR fusion field.

Careful rendering pipeline engineering: custom UE5 pipeline preserving linear HDR space, EXR storage to avoid quantization, and camera shake simulation to mimic handheld capture, improving realism over naive synthetic rendering.

The proposed S2R-Adapter is a reasonably well-motivated share/transfer branch design that supports both labeled fine-tuning and unlabeled test-time adaptation via a mean-teacher/uncertainty-driven scaling scheme, and can be re-parameterized to avoid extra inference cost.

Comprehensive experimental protocol covering labeled fine-tuning, unlabeled test-time adaptation, cross-dataset generalization, and multiple ablations (branch contributions, knowledge-forgetting analysis, TTA framework components).

Additional supplementary experiments (Kalantari, Real-HDRV datasets; dataset scale comparisons; diversity metrics via t-SNE and 7-dimensional feature statistics) provide reasonable support for the dataset diversity and utility claims.
Consistent, if sometimes modest, improvements across two backbone architectures (CNN-based SAFNet and Transformer-based SCTNet) and two real test datasets support the generality of the approach.
weaknesses: The core adapter design largely recombines existing techniques (LoRA-style low/high-rank adapters, mean-teacher TTA, uncertainty-based branch scaling from prior works such as ViDA), limiting the methodological novelty beyond adapting these ideas to the HDR fusion task.

Some reported gains are marginal or inconsistent across metrics (e.g., HDR-VDP2 improvement on SCT for SCTNet is only 69.33 vs 69.22, while PSNR gains are larger), raising questions about the robustness/significance of improvements, especially since SSIM values are already near saturation (~0.98-0.99) leaving little room to demonstrate meaningful differences.

No comparison against alternative/established sim-to-real domain adaptation baselines (e.g., adversarial domain adaptation, domain randomization) beyond internal ablations of the proposed adapter's own components, making it hard to judge whether S2R-Adapter is actually superior to other DA strategies for this task.

Evaluation is limited to two primary real-world test datasets (SCT, Challenge123), which are themselves relatively small and possibly not fully representative of real-world diversity; while appendix experiments add two more datasets, the core comparisons and ablations remain narrow.
No variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple runs, making it difficult to assess whether reported improvements (often <1 dB in several settings) are robust or within noise.

Reproducibility depends heavily on proprietary UE5 asset libraries and an internal rendering/toolkit pipeline (built on xrfeitoria); details of asset licensing, exact scene construction, and full pipeline configuration are not fully specified in the main text, and full dataset/code release is only promised, not verified.

The domain gap visualization (Fig. 2, Fig. A1) confirms persistent differences even after adaptation, particularly in texture-rich regions (trees, grass, people), suggesting the adapter only partially closes the sim-to-real gap, which is not deeply analyzed or quantified beyond qualitative difference maps.

strengths: Addresses a genuine bottleneck in HDR fusion research: existing real-world datasets with ground truth are extremely small (89-144 samples), and the proposed S2R-HDR dataset at 24,000 images is a substantial scale increase.

The rendering pipeline attends to several practical details (linear HDR/EXR output avoiding baked-in tone mapping, camera shake simulation, diverse dynamic elements including humans/animals/vehicles, varied lighting/times of day) that could be useful to the community if released.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across multiple settings: labeled fine-tuning, unlabeled test-time adaptation, and several ablations isolating the share/transfer branches and the uncertainty-based scale adjustment.

Consistent (if modest) quantitative improvements are shown across two baseline architectures (CNN-based SAFNet, Transformer-based SCTNet) and two real benchmarks (SCT, Challenge123), suggesting the proposed pipeline is not overfit to a single setting.
weaknesses: The core domain-adaptation contribution (S2R-Adapter) is a fairly direct recombination of existing techniques (LoRA-style low-rank adapters, high-rank adapters, mean-teacher test-time adaptation, uncertainty-driven branch scaling largely borrowed from ViDA) applied to a new task, with limited new conceptual insight beyond integration engineering.

Real-world test sets used for evaluation are very small (36 samples for SCT, 27 for Challenge123), making reported PSNR/SSIM gains of a few tenths of a dB difficult to trust as statistically meaningful; no variance, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported anywhere in the paper.

The 'diversity' and domain-gap analyses rely on a hand-crafted 7-dimensional feature set and t-SNE visualization borrowed wholesale from unrelated prior work; there is no validation that these metrics actually correlate with downstream fusion quality or with the true sim-to-real gap relevant to the task.

Experimental comparisons in Table 2 are not strictly apples-to-apples: competing methods are trained only on the small real datasets, while the proposed method benefits from large-scale synthetic pretraining plus fine-tuning, which is an inherent data-scale advantage rather than purely a methodological one; a baseline of 'same baseline network fine-tuned without S2R pretraining, using comparable total compute/augmentation' would better isolate the contribution.

No independent validation of rendering realism (e.g., human perceptual study, or quantitative comparison of raw rendered sensor statistics vs real raw HDR sensor data) beyond the ad hoc diversity metrics; claims of 'high quality' and 'realistic' are largely asserted rather than demonstrated.

The paper offers no discussion of dataset limitations, biases (e.g., synthetic asset diversity, demographic representation of human motion models), licensing, or potential misuse, despite claiming applications in autonomous driving and other real-world domains.

Ablation results (Tables 5-7) show quite small absolute differences between configurations (e.g., 43.20 vs 43.33 PSNR-µ), raising concern about whether the architectural choices (branch ranks, learned vs fixed scale factors) are actually impactful or within noise.

Only two network backbones (SAFNet, SCTNet) are used for the main adapter experiments, limiting evidence of generality across architectures despite claims that the method works for 'any pretrained layers' and both CNN/Transformer structures.
Some reported numbers are flagged as 'recalculated' from provided images (HDR-VDP2 in Table 2), raising reproducibility and consistency concerns with the original baseline papers.

strengths: Introduces S2R-HDR, the first large-scale (24,000 image) synthetic HDR dataset rendered via UE5, addressing a genuine bottleneck (existing real datasets have only 89-144 samples) with careful engineering (linear HDR EXR output, camera shake simulation, diverse dynamic elements including humans/animals/vehicles, varied lighting/times of day).

Proposes S2R-Adapter, a reasonably novel plug-and-play domain adaptation scheme with separate low-rank 'share' and high-rank 'transfer' branches, applicable both to labeled fine-tuning and unlabeled test-time adaptation via a mean-teacher/uncertainty-driven scheme, with no extra inference cost via re-parameterization.

Extensive experimental validation across two backbone architectures (CNN-based SAFNet, Transformer-based SCTNet), multiple real test datasets (SCT, Challenge123, and supplementary results on Kalantari and Real-HDRV), and both labeled/unlabeled adaptation settings, consistently showing SOTA improvements.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each adapter branch, learned vs. fixed scale factors, and TTA components (teacher-student framework, uncertainty-based scaling), plus a knowledge-forgetting experiment showing the adapter better preserves pretrained knowledge than naive fine-tuning.

Good supporting analyses including t-SNE visualizations of domain gap/branch behavior, diversity metrics comparison (Table 1), and detailed appendix with additional qualitative results, dataset statistics, and scale comparisons that aid reproducibility and understanding.
weaknesses: Absolute performance gains from S2R-Adapter over strong baselines in the labeled setting are relatively modest (roughly 0.6-2 dB PSNR-µ), and it is unclear how much of the improvement is attributable to the larger/more diverse pretraining data versus the adapter design itself versus simply more model capacity/parameters during fine-tuning.

The diversity/quality claims (Table 1, Fig. 2) rely on self-selected, hand-crafted 7-dimensional features and t-SNE, which can be sensitive to feature choice and rendering-induced artifacts (e.g., synthetic scenes may trivially achieve higher 'dynamic range' or 'highlight' scores due to unconstrained virtual lighting rather than reflecting genuinely more useful diversity for the fusion task).

No perceptual/human study is conducted despite strong visual-quality claims (ghosting reduction, highlight recovery); reliance solely on PSNR/SSIM/HDR-VDP2 may not fully capture perceptual artifacts that the paper emphasizes qualitatively in figures.

Real-world evaluation is concentrated on two relatively small test sets (SCT: 36 test samples, Challenge123: 27 test samples); while supplementary results add Kalantari/Real-HDRV, the core comparisons and ablations are still evaluated on limited real scene diversity, raising some concern about the robustness/generality of the reported gains.

The domain gap analysis and adapter design, while reasonable, do not compare against other established sim-to-real or TTA baselines beyond the backbone architectures' own training paradigms (e.g., no comparison with alternative adapter/PEFT or adversarial domain adaptation methods as direct baselines for the adaptation stage itself).

Some novelty concerns: the rendering pipeline builds heavily on existing tools/engines (UE5, xrfeitoria) and the adapter architecture is a fairly direct adaptation of prior share/transfer branch ideas (e.g., ViDA) to a new task, somewhat limiting the technical novelty relative to the engineering/dataset contribution.

strengths: Introduces S2R-HDR, by far the largest HDR fusion dataset to date (24,000 HDR images vs. 89-144 in prior work), rendered in linear HDR/EXR format via a custom Unreal Engine 5 pipeline that avoids baked-in tone mapping and quantization, with diverse indoor/outdoor scenes, lighting (day/twilight/night), and motion types (humans, animals, vehicles), plus camera-shake simulation for realism.

Proposes S2R-Adapter, a plug-and-play share/transfer branch adapter applicable to both CNN (SAFNet) and Transformer (SCTNet) backbones, supporting both supervised fine-tuning and test-time adaptation without ground truth via an uncertainty-driven mean-teacher scheme.

Extremely thorough empirical validation: results on SCT and Challenge123 with and without ground truth, cross-dataset generalization (Table 4), ablations isolating share/transfer branches and TTA components, knowledge-forgetting analysis (Table 7), and numerous appendix experiments (Kalantari, Real-HDRV, Sen, Tursun datasets; HDR video reconstruction with HDRFlow; runtime overhead analysis).

Consistent and often substantial quantitative gains (e.g., +0.6 to +2 dB PSNR-μ) across multiple baselines and datasets, supporting the claim that the dataset and adapter improve generalization to real scenes.

Good supplementary material: t-SNE domain-gap visualization, difference maps showing where the adapter helps (texture-rich regions), auxiliary modalities (optical flow, depth, normals) for future extensions, and a reproducibility statement with promised code/dataset release.
weaknesses: The diversity/quality metrics used to argue dataset superiority (FHLP, EHL, SI, CF, stdL, ALL, DR) are self-selected proxy measures rather than validated indicators of usefulness for downstream fusion quality; no human/perceptual study is conducted to confirm that the rendered images are perceptually realistic or that improvements are perceptually meaningful.

The S2R-Adapter design is largely a recombination of existing techniques (LoRA-style low/high-rank adapters, mean-teacher TTA, uncertainty-based scale weighting), offering limited methodological novelty beyond the dataset contribution.

Evaluation relies almost exclusively on PSNR/SSIM/HDR-VDP2 computed against synthetic or limited real ground truth; qualitative real-world results (Fig. 7, 10) lack any quantitative ground truth, making claims about real-scene generalization only partially substantiated.

Some result tables (e.g., Table 3) are visually cramped/inconsistent in formatting, making certain comparisons hard to verify precisely; a few numbers (e.g., PSNR-ℓ improvements claimed in text vs. tables) would benefit from clearer cross-referencing.

The domain gap between synthetic and real data is acknowledged but not fully closed; the adapter still requires either labeled real data or online TTA, and the residual gap (e.g., in fine textures like trees/grass/people) is only illustrated qualitatively via difference maps, not quantified.
Test-time adaptation incurs a non-trivial ~60% runtime increase per image, which could be a practical concern for real-time HDR applications such as video or mobile imaging.

The dataset construction relies partly on purchased Unreal Engine assets, which may hinder exact reproducibility of the full asset library even though the rendering pipeline itself is described as reproducible.

Comparisons omit some recent 2024-2025 HDR fusion methods cited in related work (e.g., diffusion-based or UltraFusion), limiting the completeness of the baseline comparison in the main results tables.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck in HDR fusion research: the scarcity of large-scale, ground-truth-paired dynamic-scene HDR data. The proposed S2R-HDR (24,000 images, 1,000 sequences) is substantially larger than prior datasets (89–144 samples), which is a real practical contribution to the community if released.

The rendering pipeline is carefully engineered to avoid common synthetic-data pitfalls (custom linear-space tone mapping/gamma correction, EXR float storage to avoid quantization, camera-shake simulation via Perlin noise), showing attention to making the synthetic data usable for HDR-specific training rather than a naive off-the-shelf render.

The S2R-Adapter design (shared low-rank branch + transfer high-rank branch, with scale factors tunable either via supervised fine-tuning or via an uncertainty-driven mean-teacher test-time-adaptation scheme) is a sensible application of PEFT/adapter ideas to the sim-to-real HDR problem, and is shown to be architecture-agnostic (CNN and Transformer backbones).

The empirical evaluation is broad: results are reported on SCT and Challenge123 with and without ground truth, cross-dataset generalization experiments (Table 4/8), knowledge-forgetting checks (Table 7), ablations on adapter branches and TTA components (Tables 5-6), and additional experiments extending to older datasets (Kalantari, Sen, Tursun) and even an HDR video reconstruction task, which strengthens the claim of general applicability.

The paper includes qualitative diagnostics (t-SNE domain visualization, difference maps showing where adaptation matters) that give some interpretability into what the adapter is learning, rather than relying purely on aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: The core adapter methodology is largely a recombination of existing techniques (LoRA-style low/high-rank adapters, mean-teacher self-training, uncertainty-based test-time scaling from prior TTA works) applied to a new domain; the technical novelty of S2R-Adapter itself is incremental rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Real-world evaluation is still confined to very small test sets (36 SCT samples, 27 Challenge123 samples), which is exactly the data-scarcity limitation the paper criticizes in prior work; claims of strong 'generalization' rest on a narrow real-world footprint that may not represent the full diversity the synthetic dataset targets.

In several results (e.g., Table 4/8), directly training on the matched real dataset (SCT or Challenge123) still outperforms or is very close to models pretrained on S2R-HDR plus adaptation when evaluated in-domain, so the practical benefit of the synthetic dataset is mainly for cross-domain/generalization settings rather than a universal improvement — this nuance is somewhat oversold in the text (e.g., 'achieves state-of-the-art performance').

The proposed 'diversity' and 'HDR extent' metrics (FHLP, EHL, SI, CF, stdL, ALL, DR) used to argue dataset superiority in Table 1 are self-defined/ad hoc, not independently validated against downstream task benefit, and the t-SNE-based domain-gap visualizations are qualitative rather than quantitatively conclusive.

No human/perceptual study is included despite HDR fusion quality being strongly tied to perceptual artifacts (ghosting, halos); reliance solely on PSNR/SSIM/HDR-VDP2 may not fully capture the qualitative claims made from the figures.

Reported gains are frequently modest (tenths of a dB in several tables) despite being described with strong language ('significant', 'notably'), and no variance/multiple-run statistics are provided to assess significance of these differences.

Dataset and code links are left blank/placeholder ('available at URL:'), and reproducibility of the exact asset composition is limited since some UE5 assets were purchased and may not be redistributable, raising concerns about the practical reproducibility and long-term availability of the promised resource.

The domain gap between synthetic and real data is acknowledged to persist even after the proposed rendering improvements (as shown by t-SNE and difference maps), suggesting the 'high-fidelity' claim for the raw rendered data is somewhat undercut by the continued necessity of a dedicated adapter to close a non-trivial residual gap.

strengths: Introduces S2R-HDR, by far the largest HDR fusion dataset to date (24,000 rendered HDR frames vs. 89-144 in prior work), with a carefully engineered UE5 rendering pipeline that outputs true linear HDR in EXR format (avoiding baked-in tone mapping/quantization) and simulates camera shake for realism.

Good diversity design: covers indoor/outdoor scenes, three lighting regimes (day/twilight/night), and multiple motion categories (humans, animals, vehicles), quantitatively validated against prior datasets using seven diversity/HDR-extent metrics and t-SNE visualizations.

Proposes S2R-Adapter, a lightweight, plug-and-play share/transfer branch adapter that can be used both for supervised fine-tuning on labeled real data and for test-time adaptation on unlabeled real data, and is shown to work with both CNN (SAFNet) and Transformer (SCTNet/HDR-Transformer) backbones.

Extensive experimentation: main results on two real datasets (SCT, Challenge123) with and without ground truth, plus a large appendix with additional evaluations on Kalantari, Real-HDRV, Sen, Tursun datasets, an HDR video reconstruction task (HDRFlow), TTA runtime overhead analysis, and multiple ablations (branch contributions, knowledge-forgetting comparison, dataset scale comparison).

Reasonably clear reproducibility statement with promised public release of code/dataset, and additional auxiliary modalities (optical flow, depth, normals, diffuse) that broaden potential utility beyond HDR fusion.
Qualitative results convincingly show reduced ghosting/occlusion artifacts and better recovery of extreme highlights (e.g., direct sunlight) compared to baselines trained on prior datasets.
weaknesses: The core adapter design (low-rank shared branch + high-rank transfer branch, uncertainty-based scale adjustment) is a fairly direct combination of existing PEFT/adapter and mean-teacher TTA techniques (LoRA-style adapters, ViDA, uncertainty-guided TTA) with limited new algorithmic insight; the main novelty lies in the dataset rather than the method.

Real-world test sets used for main quantitative comparisons remain small (36 test samples for SCT, 27 for Challenge123), so gains, while consistent, are measured on limited real evaluation data; broader real-world validation would strengthen the claims.

It is not entirely disentangled how much of the improvement comes from the adapter design specifically versus simply having access to a much larger and higher-quality synthetic training corpus; while Table 5 ablates the branches, a controlled comparison against naive fine-tuning with equal training budget/data scale would clarify the adapter's marginal value more rigorously.

The dataset construction relies partly on purchased UE5 assets, which the paper itself notes limits full reproducibility of the exact scene assets used, even though the pipeline/code will be released.

Discussion of failure cases or remaining limitations of the synthetic data (e.g., specular/reflective materials, complex real-world sensor noise characteristics not captured by rendering) is largely absent, despite the paper's own domain-gap analysis (Fig. 9) showing texture-rich regions like foliage and people remain problematic.

Some presentation issues: dense/small tables (especially in the appendix), minor inconsistencies/typos (e.g., legend label 'Rea Datasets' in Figure 8, 'PNSR-μ' typo in Table 9), which slightly hinder readability.
